value.overview: The Bananaquit is a tiny, active songbird of tropical habitats. It is recognized by its sharp, slightly curved bill, bold white eyebrow, dark upperparts, yellow rump and yellow underparts. Bananaquits feed mainly on flower nectar but also take fruit and small invertebrates. They are common around gardens, forest edges, scrub and open woodland, where their quick movements and high-pitched, scratchy calls often make them easier to detect than to follow.
value.classification: The Bananaquit belongs to the order Passeriformes and the tanager family, Thraupidae. It is the only species in the genus Coereba, although its taxonomic placement has historically been debated.
value.identification: This small bird measures about 10–11 cm long. Mainland birds, including those in Costa Rica, usually have dark gray upperparts, a strong white stripe above the eye, a blackish bill with a pinkish gape, gray throat, yellow rump and yellow underparts. The Bananaquit moves rapidly through vegetation and often clings sideways to flowers while feeding. Its short, scratchy or buzzy song and energetic behavior are useful clues. Plumage varies among regional populations, especially on Caribbean islands.
value.rangeHabitat: The Bananaquit ranges from southeastern Mexico through Central America and much of South America, as well as across many Caribbean islands. In Costa Rica it is a regular resident and is found in suitable habitat throughout much of the country, including lowlands, foothills and some higher elevations. It occupies forest edges, second growth, gardens, plantations, scrub, flowering vegetation and open woodland. It is especially common where dense cover and nectar-producing plants occur, rather than in unbroken mature forest alone.
value.migrationStatus: The Costa Rican population is generally resident year-round, not a regular long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability, flowering and seasonal conditions.
value.breeding: Bananaquits build untidy, enclosed, globe-shaped nests from plant fibers and other soft materials. They may construct separate roosting or dormitory nests outside the breeding period. The female generally incubates the eggs alone, while both adults feed the nestlings. Young typically leave the nest after about 17–19 days. Breeding can occur during different parts of the year across the species’ broad tropical range, and timing varies with local rainfall, food supplies and climate.
value.dietFeeding: Nectar is the main food, obtained by probing flowers with the pointed, curved bill. Bananaquits may pierce flowers at the base when this provides easier access to nectar, and they sometimes visit hummingbird feeders or sources of sugar. They also eat soft fruit and small insects or other arthropods, particularly when feeding young. Their feeding behavior may make them occasional pollinators of tropical plants.
value.behavior: The Bananaquit is fast-moving, alert and frequently restless while foraging. It commonly travels through shrubs, vines and flowering trees in pairs, family groups or alone, and may hang beneath leaves or flowers. Birds defend feeding areas and can be bold around people, gardens and outdoor dining spaces. They communicate with high, thin, scratchy notes and often remain active throughout the day. Enclosed nests may also be used as communal roosts.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered very large, although available assessments indicate that it appears to be decreasing.
